messages.subject: Multibyte string error
messages.body_plain:
I was working on the "other applications 4" assignment, the one about
using R to perform searches in Google. I didn't have any problems with
the search word "perl" or even "linux", but when I searched for
"python" I got the following error message in R:

"Error in substr(lines, starts, stops) :
invalid multibyte string at '<97>..."

I assume this error came up when the function "exact.matches" was
running, as I didn't put in the function substr() in my script and
exact.matches has it. I've received this error message before, when my
text files had "smart" quotes rather than straight ones.

My question for you R enthusiasts is: How can I get around this
multibyte string error, if I can?

Thanks. Earl Brown

messages.subject: RE: [CorpLing with R] Multibyte string error
messages.body_plain:
This looks like a character encoding issue rather than an R issue. Your
underlying encoding seems to be Windows-1252 (which has actual
characters, including "smart" punctuation marks in the range 0x80 to
0x9f: 0x97 is an emdash and the smart quotes you mention having caused
the problem before are also in this range), and the function must be
expecting UTF-8 (in which 0x97, and other characters in this range,
cannot appear alone but must always be part of a well-formed longer
sequence of characters).

The solution is to make sure to recode the string to UTF-8 before doing
anything with it. The iconv() function will do this for you. iconvlist()
tells you what encodings are available.

If Windows-1252 is not available as a supported encoding, then you can
use ISO-8859-1 instead as the "from" encoding, but in this case make
sure to set the sub argument to iconv() to something like "?", because
the characters from 0x80 to 0x9f are Microsoft-only innovations, thus
illegal in ISO-8859-1 and therefore may not convert to Unicode if the
"from" encoding is ISO-8859-1.

An alternative is to write your own function to globally switch each of
the "smart" punctuation marks for an ASCII equivalent (e.g. the straight
quotes for the smart quotes, a minus for the endash and emdash). This
has the advantage of making searches simpler later on -- if you are ever
going to be in the position of needing to search for punctuation!

Hope this is useful.

best

Andrew.

Andrew Hardie
Linguistics and English Language
Bowland College, Lancaster University
Lancaster LA1 4YT
United Kingdom

http://www.ling.lancs.ac.uk/staff/hardie

messages.subject: [CorpLing with R] Column alignment
messages.body_plain:
Hello R-ists,

Does anyone know of a way to specify the alignment (right, left,
center, etc.) of individual columns in a data frame printed to
screen?

I've loaded a data frame with read.table() and then pulled out and put
together a few individual columns from that data frame with
data.frame(), and then used print() to print them to screen. The
function print() takes the argument "right=T", which controls all
columns. But, if possible, I'd like to have the first column be right-
aligned, the second center-aligned, and the third left-aligned when it
prints to screen in the console. (I know that this can easily be done
in a spreadsheet, but how about in the R console itself?)

Thanks for your time and help. Still loving R. Earl Brown

messages.subject: [CorpLing with R] Correcting text-processed data
messages.body_plain:
As we probably all know, text copied from Microsoft Word and some other programs and pasted into an ASCII text file differs from words typed there natively, particularly where apostrophes are concerned. The word "don't," for example, comes out as "don¡¯t". In the corpus I'm working with, some contributions are like this, but not all.

So is there a way we can use R to go through a corpus and replace the "corrupted" version with the intended ASCII version? Of course I could make a list of all such corrupted words and replace them all. If it were just a matter of contractions I might make the effort since this is a finite set, but this also includes the possessive form of proper nouns. Is there a one-size-fits-all approach that will find and correct all such instances?

--
Kevin Parent, Ph.D

National Korea Toastmasters webmaster www.koreatoastmasters.ning.com <http://www.koreatoastmasters.ning.com>
